items.title: Step 1
items.description:
In this workshop, you will build a sentence analyzer that will take a sentence and get the count for the number of words, vowels, consonants, and punctuation marks.

To begin, create a `getVowelCount` function with a parameter called `sentence`. Your function should return the total number of vowels in a sentence.

hints.text: You should create a `getVowelCount` function.
Your `getVowelCount` function should have a `sentence` parameter.
Your `getVowelCount` function should return a number.
When the sentence is `"Apples are tasty fruits"`, the `getVowelCount` function should return `7`.
When the sentence is `"Hello, World!"`, the function should return `3`.
Your vowel count should be case-insensitive.
hints.test:
assert.strictEqual(getVowelCount("Apples are tasty fruits"), 7);
assert.strictEqual(getVowelCount("freeCodeCamp is awesome"), 10);

hints.text: Your `getVowelCount` function should return the correct vowel count for any sentence.

items.title: Step 2
items.description:
Now it is time to test your `getVowelCount` function.

Create a `vowelCount` variable and assign it the result of calling the `getVowelCount` function with the argument of `"Apples are tasty fruits"`

After that, log the following to the console: `"Vowel Count: [vowel count goes here]"`. Replace  `[vowel count goes here]` with the actual variable name. You can choose to use template strings or string concatenation with the `+` operator here.

hints.text: You should create a `vowelCount` variable.
Your `vowelCount` variable should be set to the result of `getVowelCount("Apples are tasty fruits")`.
You should log the `vowelCount` variable to the console with the parameter `"Vowel Count: ${vowelCount}"`.

items.title: Step 3
items.description:
It's time to count the consonants. Create a `getConsonantCount` function with a `sentence` parameter.

Inside the function, use a loop to count the number of consonants in the `sentence` that will be passed into the function when it is called. A consonant is any letter that is not one of the following characters: `"aeiou"`. 

Your `getConsonantCount` function must return a number.

hints.text: You should create a `getConsonantCount` function.
Your `getConsonantCount` function should have a `sentence` parameter.
Your `getConsonantCount` function should return a number.
When the sentence is `"Coding is fun"`, the `getConsonantCount` function should return `7`.
When the sentence is `"Hello, World!"`, the `getConsonantCount` function should return `7`.
Your consonant count should be case-insensitive.
Your `getConsonantCount` function should return the correct consonant count for any sentence.

items.title: Step 4
items.description:
Now it is time to test your `getConsonantCount` function.

Create a `consonantCount` variable and assign it the result of calling the `getConsonantCount` function with the argument of `"Coding is fun"`

After that, log the following to the console: `"Consonant Count: [Consonant count goes here]"`. Replace  `[Consonant count goes here]` with the actual variable name. You can choose to use template strings or string concatenation with the `+` operator here.

hints.text: You should create a `consonantCount` variable.
Your `consonantCount` variable should be set to the result of `getConsonantCount("Coding is fun")`.
You should log the `consonantCount` variable to the console with the parameter `"Consonant Count: ${consonantCount}"`.

items.title: Step 5
items.description:
You should count the number of punctuations now.

Create a `getPunctuationCount` function with a `sentence` parameter.

Inside the function, create a loop to count the number of punctuation characters in the `sentence` that will be passed into the function when it is called. For our purposes, a punctuation character is any character that is not a space (`" "`) or a letter.

Your `getPunctuationCount` function must return a number.

hints.text: You should create a `getPunctuationCount` function.
Your `getPunctuationCount` function should have a `sentence` parameter.
Your `getPunctuationCount` function should return a number.
When the sentence is `"What's going on here?"`, the `getPunctuationCount` function should return `2`.
When the sentence is `"What????!"`, the `getPunctuationCount` function should return `5`.
Your `getPunctuationCount` function should return the correct punctuation count for any sentence.

items.title: Step 6
items.description:
Now it is time to test your `getPunctuationCount` function.

Create a `punctuationCount` variable and assign it the result of calling the `getPunctuationCount` function with the argument of `"WHAT?!?!?!?!?"`

After that, log the following to the console: `"Punctuation Count: [Punctuation count goes here]"`. Replace  `[Punctuation count goes here]` with the actual variable name. You can choose to use template strings or string concatenation with the `+` operator here.

hints.text: You should create a `punctuationCount` variable.
Your `punctuationCount` variable should be set to the result of `getPunctuationCount("WHAT?!?!?!?!?")`.

You should log the following to the console: `"Punctuation Count: [Punctuation count goes here]"`. Replace  `[Punctuation count goes here]` with the actual variable name. Make sure to use proper string concatenation syntax here.

items.title: Step 7
items.description: Finally, count the number of words by creating a `getWordCount` function with a `sentence` parameter. The function should return the total number of words in the sentence passed in when it is called.

hints.text: You should create a `getWordCount` function.
Your `getWordCount` function should have a `sentence` parameter.
Your `getWordCount` function should return a number.
When the sentence is `"When are you gonna start learning to code?"`, the `getWordCount` function should return `8`.
hints.test: assert.strictEqual(getWordCount("When are you gonna start learning to code?"), 8);

hints.text: When the sentence is `"What's going on?"`, the `getWordCount` function should return `3`.
Your word count should be case-insensitive.
hints.test:
assert.strictEqual(getWordCount("freeCodeCamp offers free coding tutorials online"), 6);
assert.strictEqual(getWordCount("You can learn HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and more on freeCodeCamp"), 10);

hints.text: Your `getWordCount` function should return the correct word count for any sentence.
Your `getWordCount` function should return the correct word count for an empty string, or a string only with spaces.

items.title: Step 8
items.description:
Test your `getWordCount` by creating a `wordCount` variable set to the calling of the `getWordCount` function with the sentence `"I love freeCodeCamp"`.

After that, log the following to the console: `"Word Count: [Word count goes here]"`. Replace  `[Word count goes here]` with the actual variable name. You can choose to use template strings or string concatenation with the `+` operator here.

With that, your sentence analyzer project is done!

hints.text: You should create a `wordCount` variable.
Your `wordCount` variable should be set to the result of `getWordCount("I love freeCodeCamp")`.
You should log the `wordCount` variable to the console with the parameter `"Word Count: ${wordCount}"`.
